For fixed step sizes, define
\[
p(\lambda)=\prod_{k=0}^2(1-\alpha_k\lambda).
\]
Since \(A\) is real symmetric, it is orthogonally diagonalizable, so
\[
\frac{\|x_3\|_2}{\|x_0\|_2}
=\frac{\|p(A)x_0\|_2}{\|x_0\|_2}
\]
has worst case
\[
\max_{\lambda\in[1,4]\cup[6,9]} |p(\lambda)|.
\]
Conversely, a one-dimensional matrix \(A=[\lambda]\) shows this maximum is actually attained in the outer supremum. Thus the problem is the minimax problem for cubics \(p\) with \(p(0)=1\) coming from positive roots.

For any cubic \(p\), interpolate \(p(0)\) from the four values at \(1,3,7,9\):
\[
p(0)=\frac{63}{32}p(1)-\frac{21}{16}p(3)+\frac{9}{16}p(7)-\frac{7}{32}p(9).
\]
Therefore, if \(|p|\le M\) on the two intervals, then
\[
1=|p(0)|
\le \left(\frac{63}{32}+\frac{21}{16}+\frac{9}{16}+\frac{7}{32}\right)M
=\frac{65}{16}M.
\]
Hence
\[
M\ge \frac{16}{65}.
\]

Now take
\[
p_*(x)=\frac{65-63x+15x^2-x^3}{65}.
\]
Then
\[
p_*'(x)=-\frac{3}{65}(x-3)(x-7).
\]
Also
\[
p_*(1)=\frac{16}{65},\quad
p_*(3)=-\frac{16}{65},\quad
p_*(7)=\frac{16}{65},\quad
p_*(9)=-\frac{16}{65},
\]
and
\[
p_*(4)=-\frac{11}{65},\qquad p_*(6)=\frac{11}{65}.
\]
The derivative sign shows these are the only possible extrema on \([1,4]\cup[6,9]\), so
\[
\max_{\lambda\in[1,4]\cup[6,9]} |p_*(\lambda)|=\frac{16}{65}.
\]

Finally,
\[
65-63x+15x^2-x^3
=-(x-5)(x^2-10x+13),
\]
so the roots of \(p_*\) are
\[
5-2\sqrt3,\qquad 5,\qquad 5+2\sqrt3.
\]
Thus the step sizes are their reciprocals, ordered increasingly:
\[
\alpha_0^*=\frac1{5+2\sqrt3}=\frac{5-2\sqrt3}{13},\quad
\alpha_1^*=\frac15,\quad
\alpha_2^*=\frac1{5-2\sqrt3}=\frac{5+2\sqrt3}{13}.
\]

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\frac{16}{65},
\left(\frac{5-2\sqrt3}{13},\frac15,\frac{5+2\sqrt3}{13}\right)
\right)
}
\]
